newsitem.title: USA: Dallas paper says to publish no new McVeigh articles.
newsitem.headline: Dallas paper says to publish no new McVeigh articles.

text.p: The Dallas Morning News, which reported that Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh had admitted planting the bomb that killed 168 people, said on Monday it would publish no new articles based on confidential defence documents.
The newspaper said its decision was due to consideration of McVeigh's right to a fair trial.
The move followed warnings by lead defence attorney Stephen Jones that the paper's report might force him to request a delay in McVeigh's trial, which is scheduled to begin on March 31.

The Dallas Morning News reported on Friday that McVeigh had told his defence team he planted the bomb that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in downtown Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995 and that he had aimed for a busy time of the day to get a "body count" that would send a strong message to the government.
The newspaper cited defence documents, but Jones dismissed the report as false and suggested that the newspaper might be the victim of an elaborate hoax.
The Morning News said on Monday it would publish no more reports based on the defence documents, although it continued to stand by the original stories.

"The Dallas Morning News remains sensitive to the tension between Mr. McVeigh's fair trial rights and the national public interest in this case," it said in a document that was to be filed on Monday before the Denver court where McVeigh is to go on trial.

"The News published ... information it believed served a compelling public interest. It has no further plans to report the unpublished information from the material used as the source of the previous articles," the newspaper said.

Ralph Langer, the newspaper's executive vice president, said the original story was of overriding public significance but that "any further articles based on the defence reports would not rise to the same level of importance.".
In an interview on ABC-TV's "This Week" programme on Sunday, Jones said he had not asked to relocate the trial but that a delay might be necessary.
"It will be an enormous expense and inconvenience, to say nothing of an emotional impact on the victims and others, if this trial is delayed," he said.
Citing a gag order imposed by the judge and limits on what he could say as a defence lawyer, Jones would not say whether some elements in the Dallas newspaper report may be true.
"The only way that I can tell you in answer to that question... is to say, one, Mr. McVeigh has pled not guilty and, two, the defence will not present a false defence," he said.

According to The Dallas Morning News report, McVeigh implicated his co-defendant, Terry Nichols, in the bomb plot but told his defence team that he alone drove the explosives-filled truck that destroyed the federal building.
